title: What are distributed transactions using JTA and XA with two-phase commit? Why are they discouraged in microservices, and what are the alternatives like Saga, the Outbox pattern, and eventual consistency?
shortTitle: What are distributed transactions and why is Saga preferred?

s1_definition.profdef: A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, such as two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them atomically. The classic mechanism is JTA (the Java Transaction API) coordinating XA-compliant resources using two-phase commit. In phase one, a coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote; in phase two, if all voted yes, it tells them all to commit, otherwise all to roll back. In microservices this is discouraged because it couples services tightly, holds locks across network calls, scales poorly, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The common alternatives are the Saga pattern, the transactional Outbox pattern, and designing for eventual consistency.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must move money and, at the same instant, update a separate insurance system. Two-phase commit is like a wedding officiant asking both the bride and groom "do you agree?" and only finalizing the marriage if both say yes. The problem is everyone must stand frozen at the altar holding their breath (holding locks) while the officiant waits for slow replies over the phone. If the officiant faints mid-ceremony (coordinator crash), everyone is stuck. In microservices we instead do the steps one at a time and, if a later step fails, we run a "sorry, undo that" step — that is Saga.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two-phase commit gives strict atomicity across resources but holds locks across the network and needs a coordinator, so microservices prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, such as two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them atomically. The classic mechanism is JTA (the Java Transaction API) coordinating XA-compliant resources using two-phase commit. In phase one, a coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote; in phase two, if all voted yes, it tells them all to commit, otherwise all to roll back. In microservices this is discouraged because it couples services tightly, holds locks across network calls, scales poorly, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. The common alternatives are the Saga pattern, the transactional Outbox pattern, and designing for eventual consistency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must move money and, at the same instant, update a separate insurance system. Two-phase commit is like a wedding officiant asking both the bride and groom "do you agree?" and only finalizing the marriage if both say yes. The problem is everyone must stand frozen at the altar holding their breath (holding locks) while the officiant waits for slow replies over the phone. If the officiant faints mid-ceremony (coordinator crash), everyone is stuck. In microservices we instead do the steps one at a time and, if a later step fails, we run a "sorry, undo that" step — that is Saga.

**One line to remember:** Two-phase commit gives strict atomicity across resources but holds locks across the network and needs a coordinator, so microservices prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency.

sections.s2_technical:
JTA is the Java standard for transactions that span multiple resources. An XA resource is one that supports the XA protocol, which lets an external transaction manager coordinate its commit. A JTA transaction manager like Atomikos or Narayana coordinates these resources. In Spring you would use a `JtaTransactionManager` instead of the usual `DataSourceTransactionManager`. For example, enlisting two XA data sources means a single `@Transactional` method can write to two databases and have them commit together.

Two-phase commit is the protocol underneath. In phase one, the prepare phase, the coordinator asks each resource "can you commit?" Each resource does all the work, writes it to a durable log, locks the rows, and votes yes or no but does not commit yet. In phase two, the commit phase, if every resource voted yes the coordinator tells them all to commit; if any voted no it tells them all to roll back. The guarantee is strong atomicity across all resources.

The problem is the cost. Between phase one and phase two, every resource holds its locks and keeps its transaction open across network round-trips. If the coordinator is slow or a resource is far away, those locks are held for a long time, which kills throughput under load. For a busy bank processing thousands of transfers per second, holding row locks across a network call to another service is unacceptable.

The bigger problem in microservices is coupling and availability. Two-phase commit requires all participants to be available at commit time. If one service is down, the whole transaction cannot complete. This violates the independence that microservices are built for. The coordinator is also a single point of failure: if it crashes after phase one but before phase two, resources are left in an uncertain "in doubt" state, holding locks until the coordinator recovers. Many cloud data stores and message brokers like Kafka do not support XA at all, so you often cannot use two-phase commit even if you wanted to.

The preferred alternative is the Saga pattern. A Saga breaks one big distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each in its own service, each committing independently. If a later step fails, the Saga runs compensating transactions to undo the earlier steps. For example, a transfer across services might be: debit Rajesh's account (local commit), then credit Priya's account (local commit); if the credit fails, run a compensating transaction that credits Rajesh back. There is no global lock and no coordinator holding everything open.

Sagas come in two styles. Orchestration uses a central coordinator service that tells each step what to do next and triggers compensations on failure, which is easier to reason about and monitor. Choreography has each service publish events that the next service listens for, with no central brain, which is more decoupled but harder to trace end to end.

The Outbox pattern solves a subtle problem: you cannot atomically write to your database and publish to Kafka in one transaction because Kafka is not XA. Instead, in the same local database transaction, you write your business row and also insert a row into an outbox table. Because both writes are in the same local transaction, they commit together atomically. A separate relay process then reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, marking them sent. This guarantees that the event is published if and only if the business data committed, giving you at-least-once delivery without any distributed transaction.

All of this accepts eventual consistency. Instead of everything being perfectly consistent at the same instant, the system becomes consistent after a short delay as the steps and events propagate. For a bank, this means the transfer completes in steps and the final state is correct, even if for a brief moment one service has updated and another has not. A senior engineer designs idempotent operations and compensations so retries are safe, because in an eventually consistent system messages can be delivered more than once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a cross-service money transfer touches two separate services with two separate databases: the Account Service that holds Rajesh's savings account and the Account Service instance that holds Priya's current account, which in a microservice world are independent. We want the money to leave Rajesh and arrive at Priya atomically. The old approach was JTA two-phase commit across both databases, but it held locks across the network and the coordinator became a bottleneck and a single point of failure. This is exactly why we move to a Saga.

Problem 2 — If the debit from Rajesh succeeds but the credit to Priya fails, we must not leave the money in limbo. This is exactly what a compensating transaction does — we credit Rajesh back to undo the debit.

Problem 3 — We also need to publish a "transfer completed" event to Kafka, but we cannot write to our database and publish to Kafka in one atomic step because Kafka is not XA. This is exactly what the Outbox pattern solves — we write the business change and an outbox row in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes it afterward.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds balance with debit and credit. Two repositories stand in for two services' databases. A `TransferSaga` orchestrates: step one debits Rajesh with a local commit and writes an outbox row, step two credits Priya with a local commit; if step two fails, it runs the compensating transaction to credit Rajesh back. An `OutboxRelay` later publishes the outbox rows. The demo runs a successful Saga and a failing Saga that triggers compensation, showing eventual consistency and no global lock.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.30,000 from SAV2001 to an invalid account FROZEN9.

Step 1. The successful Saga starts. Step one debits Rajesh Rs.50,000 in its own local transaction and, in the same transaction, writes an outbox row saying "DEBITED SAV2001". This local transaction commits on its own. No global lock is held.

Step 2. Step two credits Priya Rs.50,000 in its own local transaction and writes an outbox row "CREDITED CUR3001". It commits. The Saga is complete. Rajesh is at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000.

Step 3. Later, out of band, the Outbox relay reads the unsent outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka, then marks them sent. This is the eventual consistency moment — the event reaches downstream consumers a little after the money moved.

Step 4. The failing Saga starts. Step one debits Rajesh Rs.30,000 and commits locally. Rajesh is temporarily at Rs.920,000.

Step 5. Step two tries to credit FROZEN9, which does not exist, so it throws. The Saga catches this and runs the compensating transaction, crediting Rajesh back Rs.30,000. Rajesh returns to Rs.950,000. The system is consistent again, with no money lost and no global lock ever held.

```
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] === Successful Saga ===
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] [LOCAL COMMIT] debit SAV2001 Rs.50000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] [LOCAL COMMIT] credit CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] Saga COMPLETE SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] [RELAY->Kafka] DEBITED SAV2001 Rs.50000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] [RELAY->Kafka] CREDITED CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] === Failing Saga (credit step fails) ===
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] [LOCAL COMMIT] debit SAV2001 Rs.30000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [SEVERE ] Saga step 2 failed: Account not found: FROZEN9 -> compensating
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [WARNING] [COMPENSATE] refunded SAV2001 Rs.30000
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] Saga COMPENSATED, system consistent again
2026-10-23 16:10:01 [INFO   ] FINAL Rajesh = 950000
```

```
  │  - outbox: OutboxRepository           │
  │  + debit(id, amt): void   @Transactional (+ outbox)
  │  + credit(id, amt): void  @Transactional (+ outbox)
  │  + compensateDebit(id,amt): void       compensation
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                  │ writes
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ OutboxRepository │   │  OutboxRelay          │  separate poller
  │ + add(), unsent()│   │  + publishPending()   │  → Kafka, mark sent
  └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Saga lifecycle ──────────────────────────

  [STARTED] ──debit ok──→ [DEBITED] ──credit ok──→ [COMPLETED]
                              │
                       credit fails
                              ▼
                        [COMPENSATING] ──refund──→ [COMPENSATED]

  Contrast: XA 2PC states = [PREPARE vote] → [COMMIT/ABORT],
  but coordinator crash after PREPARE → [IN_DOUBT] (locks held!)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. Controller → TransferSaga.transfer(SAV2001,CUR3001,50000)
  2.   → AccountService.debit(SAV2001)   LOCAL COMMIT + outbox
  3.   → AccountService.credit(CUR3001)  LOCAL COMMIT + outbox
  4.   → (on failure) compensateDebit(SAV2001)
  5. OutboxRelay.publishPending() → Kafka (later, eventual)

  Contract for transfer():
    Pre:  from has sufficient balance
    Post: both committed, OR debit compensated (money conserved)
    No global lock, no coordinator, tolerant of service downtime
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed transaction spans more than one resource, like two databases or a database and a message broker, and must commit or roll back all of them together. The classic way is JTA coordinating XA resources with two-phase commit. In phase one the coordinator asks every resource to prepare and vote, and in phase two it tells them all to commit if everyone voted yes or roll back if anyone voted no. That gives strict atomicity, but between the two phases every resource holds its locks and keeps its transaction open across network calls.

That cost is why two-phase commit is discouraged in microservices. Holding row locks across a network round-trip destroys throughput under load, every participant must be available at commit time which breaks the independence of services, and the coordinator is a single point of failure. If it crashes between phase one and phase two, resources are left in doubt holding locks until it recovers. On top of that, many modern stores and Kafka do not even support XA, so two-phase commit is often not an option.

In my banking project we moved a cross-service transfer from JTA to a Saga. We broke it into local transactions: debit Rajesh in his service with a local commit, then credit Priya in her service with a local commit. If the credit failed, we ran a compensating transaction that credited Rajesh back, so no money was ever lost and no global lock was ever held. We used an orchestration Saga with a central coordinator because it was easier to monitor and trace than choreography.

We combined this with the Outbox pattern, because we could not atomically write to our database and publish to Kafka. In the same local transaction we wrote the business change and an outbox row, so they committed together, and a separate relay published the outbox rows to Kafka afterward. That gave us reliable at-least-once publishing without any distributed transaction. The tradeoff we accepted was eventual consistency, so we made every operation and compensation idempotent so retries were safe. The way I summarize it in an interview is that two-phase commit buys strict atomicity at the price of availability and scale, and in microservices we almost always prefer Saga plus Outbox with eventual consistency and idempotency instead.

---

keyPoints: JTA/XA 2PC: two-phase commit across multiple databases — slow, fragile
Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions
Choreography: events trigger next step. Orchestration: central coordinator
Saga is preferred in microservices — 2PC does not scale
